<reason>A won by staying glued to the motion as written: it forced (via the best pressure question of the debate) and then monetized in every later speech B's concession that new-build delivers roughly zero in-window — a burden B could only absorb with an unquantified "portfolio average" defense that softens the motion's conjunctive text. A ran a coherent tournament-long theme (extension buys stasis, not reduction; renewables bank cumulative in-window displacement while firming costs fall), handled pressure elegantly (gracefully taking the outage correction and converting it into the "zero new generation" point; defusing B's contradiction charge with "same fact wearing two hats"), and its storage-undercutting-peakers answers left B's firming case undefended after R2. B fought superbly — the counterfactual-parity defense and especially the closing two-jobs bottleneck were the strongest substantive moves — but B's path required stacking interpretive reads, and its own closing ceded the "reducer" role to renewables, which A's final enabler/fork pounce weaponized against the motion's verb. A offered the cleaner, simpler decision rule with more independent live planks.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive sequence ran from B's Q2 through both closings: B exposed A's tension (closure as market verdict vs. closure as harmless clean backfill); A answered with the "cost verdict/emissions verdict" synthesis; B's closing then converted A's clean-backfill concession into the two-jobs bottleneck — renewable dollars can't backfill retiring reactors and displace fossil at once — the single most damaging mechanism in the debate; A's closing countered by recasting that very architecture as a confession ("nuclear as enabler, renewables as reducer... one side's dollar reduces, the other side's dollar applauds"), anchoring final weighing to the motion's verb while B's new-build concession stood unneutralized.</best_rebuttal>
